l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ and an apostle set apart for the Good News of God, greets the believers in Rome, identifying Jesus as David's offspring according to the flesh and as Son of God declared with power by the resurrection. He thanks God that the Romans' faith is proclaimed throughout the world, says he prays for them constantly and longs to visit them to impart a spiritual gift and be mutually encouraged. He explains that he has often planned to come but been hindered, and says he is a debtor to Greeks and foreigners, wise and foolish alike, and eager to preach in Rome. He declares he is not ashamed of the Good News, the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, in which God's righteousness is revealed from faith to faith. He then states that God's wrath is revealed against people who suppress the truth, who knew God through creation yet worshiped images and creatures, and whom God gave up to uncleanness, same-sex passions, a reprobate mind, and a long list of vices.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: Paul introduces himself as a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle and set apart for the Good News of God, through whom he received grace and apostleship among all nations. He thanks God for the Romans, prays for them unceasingly, longs to visit them, and says he has often been hindered. He declares himself a debtor to Greeks and foreigners, wise and foolish, and not ashamed of the Good News.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is described as God's Son, born of David's offspring according to the flesh and declared Son of God with power by the resurrection from the dead. He is called 'our Lord', and through him Paul received grace and apostleship; grace and peace come from God the Father and from him.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: God is the one who promised the Good News beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures and who is Paul's witness and the one he serves in his spirit. He reveals his righteousness in the Good News and his wrath from heaven against ungodliness, and he made himself known through creation. He gave those who rejected him up to uncleanness, vile passions, and a reprobate mind.

l: Rome, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: Rome is the city where the letter's recipients live, who are beloved of God and called to be saints. Paul is eager to preach the Good News there and hopes to come to them, having been hindered so far.

l: believers in Rome (the recipients of Paul's letter), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: The believers in Rome are addressed as beloved of God, called to belong to Jesus Christ and called to be saints. Their faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world, and Paul longs to impart a spiritual gift to them so that they and he may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith.

l: the Good News, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: The Good News is the message of God concerning his Son, promised beforehand through the prophets in the Scriptures. Paul is set apart for it and eager to preach it in Rome. It is the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first and also the Greek, and in it God's righteousness is revealed.

l: righteousness of God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: God's righteousness is said to be revealed in the Good News from faith to faith. Paul supports this by quoting the text, 'the righteous shall live by faith.'

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: The Romans' faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world, and Paul says he and they will be encouraged by each other's faith. Faith is the means by which the Good News brings salvation to everyone who believes, and by which the righteous shall live. Paul's apostleship aims at the obedience of faith among all nations.

l: God's wrath, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth. Its expression includes God giving them up to uncleanness, vile passions, and a reprobate mind, with the text stating that those who practice such things are worthy of death.

l: ungodly people who suppress the truth, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: These people knew God through what was revealed to them and through creation, yet did not glorify him or give thanks, became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise they became fools, and God gave them up to uncleanness, vile passions, and a reprobate mind. They not only practice the listed wrongs, knowing God's ordinance, but approve of others who do.

l: idolatry, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: Idolatry is described as trading the glory of the incorruptible God for images resembling corruptible man, birds, four-footed animals, and creeping things. It is also described as exchanging the truth of God for a lie and worshiping the creature rather than the Creator. God gave people up to uncleanness as a result.

l: same-sex relations, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: The text says that, as part of God giving people up to vile passions, women changed natural function into that which is against nature, and men left the natural function of the woman and burned in lust toward one another. It states that those men received in themselves the due penalty of their error.

l: vices, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 1
s: The text lists vices of those given up to a reprobate mind: unrighteousness, sexual immorality, wickedness, covetousness, malice, envy, murder, strife, deceit, evil habits, slander, backbiting, hatefulness to God, insolence, arrogance, boastfulness, inventing evil things, disobedience to parents, senselessness, covenant breaking, lack of natural affection, unforgiveness, and unmercifulness. It says those who practice such things are worthy of death, and that people both do them and approve of others who do.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 addresses the man who judges others, saying he is without excuse because he practices the same things and will not escape God's judgment. God's goodness is meant to lead to repentance, and God will pay back everyone according to their works, with wrath for the self-seeking and glory, honor, and peace for those who do good, Jew first and also Greek. Because God shows no partiality, those who sinned without the law perish without it and those under the law are judged by it, while Gentiles who do the law's things by nature are a law to themselves through conscience. The text then turns to the Jew who bears the name, rests on the law, and teaches others, but who steals, commits adultery, and dishonors God by disobeying the law, so that God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles. It concludes that circumcision profits only for a doer of the law, and that a true Jew is one inwardly, with circumcision of the heart, in the spirit, whose praise is from God.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 2
s: God's judgment is according to truth, and he shows no partiality, paying back everyone according to their works. His goodness, forbearance, and patience lead people to repentance, and he will judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ. His name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of the lawbreaking Jew, and he is the source of praise for the inward Jew.

l: Jews, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 2
s: The Jew is addressed as one who bears the name, rests on the law, glories in God, and sees himself as a guide of the blind and teacher of babies. He is charged with failing to practice what he teaches, including stealing, adultery, and robbing temples, causing God's name to be blasphemed among the Gentiles. A true Jew is redefined as one inwardly, with circumcision of the heart, whose praise comes from God. Wrath and glory both come to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 2
s: Gentiles who don't have the law are said to do by nature the things of the law, and so are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, with conscience and thoughts accusing or excusing them. God's name is blasphemed among them because of the Jew's disobedience, and the physically uncircumcised who fulfill the law will judge the lawbreaking Jew.

l: law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 2
s: The law is something Jews hear, rest on, and are instructed by, giving the form of knowledge and truth. Hearing it does not make one righteous; only doers of the law will be justified. Those who sin under it are judged by it, and its work is shown written in Gentiles' hearts.

l: judgment of God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 2
s: God's judgment is according to truth and is righteous, and it falls on those who practice evil, whether Jew or Greek. Hardened, unrepentant people store up wrath for the day of wrath. It rewards well-doing with eternal life, glory, honor, and peace, and will judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ.

l: man (the one who judges), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 2
s: The man who judges others is told he is without excuse because he condemns himself by practicing the same things. He is asked whether he thinks he will escape God's judgment, or whether he despises God's goodness, forbearance, and patience. His hard and unrepentant heart is said to be treasuring up wrath for himself.

l: circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 2
s: Circumcision profits if one is a doer of the law, but for a transgressor it becomes uncircumcision. An uncircumcised person who keeps the law's ordinances will have his uncircumcision accounted as circumcision. True circumcision is declared to be of the heart, in the spirit and not the letter, rather than outward in the flesh.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 opens with an imagined objector asking what advantage the Jew has, and answers that the Jews were entrusted with God's revelations, and that some Jews' lack of faith does not nullify God's faithfulness. The text rejects the argument that human unrighteousness or lies, by showing God's righteousness, should excuse sinners, since God must judge the world. It declares that Jews and Greeks alike are under sin, supported by a chain of quoted scriptures saying no one is righteous. The law speaks to those under it so that every mouth is closed, and no one is justified by works of the law, which only brings knowledge of sin. Apart from the law, God's righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, since all have sinned; they are justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ, whom God sent as an atoning sacrifice. Boasting is excluded, God justifies both circumcised and uncircumcised by faith, and faith establishes the law rather than nullifying it.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: God is said to be found true even if every man is a liar, and his faithfulness is not nullified by unbelief. He judges the world, is the God of both Jews and Gentiles, and sent Christ Jesus as an atoning sacrifice to demonstrate his righteousness, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ is the one through whom the righteousness of God comes by faith to all who believe. God sent him as an atoning sacrifice through faith in his blood, and the redemption that is in him is the means by which people are justified freely by grace.

l: Jews, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: The Jews have much advantage because they were entrusted with the revelations of God. Even so, they are no better than others: Jews and Greeks alike are under sin, and God, who justifies the circumcised by faith, is not the God of Jews only.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: Gentiles, called Greeks in places, are said along with Jews to be all under sin. God is their God also, and he justifies the uncircumcised through faith.

l: law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: The law speaks to those under it so that every mouth is closed and the whole world is brought under God's judgment, and through it comes the knowledge of sin. No flesh is justified by works of the law, yet the righteousness of God is testified by the law and the prophets, and faith does not nullify the law but establishes it.

l: righteousness of God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: The righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, though testified by the law and the prophets. It comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe, and God demonstrated it through the passing over of prior sins and at the present time, so that he is himself just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: Faith is the means by which the righteousness of God reaches all who believe, and by which a man is justified apart from works of the law. It excludes boasting as a law of faith, and through it God justifies both circumcised and uncircumcised.

l: justification, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: No flesh will be justified in God's sight by works of the law. Instead, people are justified freely by his grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus, and a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

l: sin, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 3
s: All, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, and the text quotes scripture that no one is righteous, no one does good, and there is no fear of God before their eyes. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and the law brings the knowledge of sin.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 takes up what Abraham, called our forefather, found according to the flesh, and argues that he was counted righteous by faith and not by works. It cites Scripture ("Abraham believed God") and David's blessing on the one whom God counts righteous apart from works. It argues that this righteousness was credited before Abraham was circumcised, so he is father both of the uncircumcised who believe and of the circumcised who walk in his faith. The promise that he would be heir of the world came through the righteousness of faith, not the law, so that it would be by grace and sure to all his offspring. The chapter ends with Abraham's unwavering faith in God, who gives life to the dead, and says that righteousness will likewise be accounted to those who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for trespasses and raised for justification.

l: Abraham, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: Abraham is called our forefather and is shown to have been counted righteous because he believed God, not because of works. He received circumcision as a seal of the righteousness he had while uncircumcised, and he becomes father of many nations and of all who believe. Though about a hundred years old and with Sarah's womb dead, he did not waver but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God and being fully assured that God could perform what he promised.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: God justifies the ungodly, counts righteousness apart from works, and will by no means charge sin to the one he blesses. He gives life to the dead and calls things that are not as though they were. He made a promise to Abraham, is able to perform it, and raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: Faith is what was accounted to Abraham for righteousness, and it is likewise accounted as righteousness to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly. Because the promise rests on faith, it is according to grace and sure to all Abraham's offspring. Abraham's faith did not weaken, and he grew strong through faith in the face of his own body's deadness and Sarah's womb.

l: justification, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: Righteousness is credited to Abraham because he believed God, and is counted by God apart from works. It was counted while he was in uncircumcision, and circumcision was a seal of it. It will also be accounted to those who believe in him who raised Jesus from the dead.

l: works, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: Works are set against faith as a basis for justification. If Abraham were justified by works he would have something to boast about, though not toward God, and the reward for one who works is counted as something owed, not as grace. David pronounces blessing on the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works.

l: law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: The promise that Abraham would be heir of the world did not come through the law. If those of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise is of no effect. The law produces wrath, since where there is no law there is no disobedience.

l: circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: Circumcision was received by Abraham as a sign and a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised. Righteousness was not counted to him in circumcision. Abraham is father of the circumcised who also walk in the steps of his faith.

l: uncircumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: Abraham's faith was accounted to him for righteousness while he was in uncircumcision, not in circumcision. This makes him father of all who believe though uncircumcised, so that righteousness may be accounted to them also. The blessing is therefore not pronounced only on the circumcised.

l: promise, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 4
s: The promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world came through the righteousness of faith, not the law. It is of faith so that it may be according to grace and sure to all the offspring, both those of the law and those of Abraham's faith. It includes the word "So will your offspring be," which Abraham believed against hope, and he was fully assured that God was able to perform it.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 says that believers, justified by faith, have peace with God through Jesus Christ and rejoice in hope and even in suffering, which leads through perseverance and proven character to hope. It shows God's love in Christ dying for the weak, ungodly, sinners and enemies, so that believers are reconciled and will be saved from God's wrath by his life. It then contrasts Adam, through whose trespass sin and death entered and reigned over all, with Jesus Christ, whose one act of righteousness and obedience brings abundant grace, the gift of righteousness, and life. The law came in so that the trespass might abound, but grace abounded more, to reign through righteousness to eternal life.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Jesus Christ is the one through whom believers have peace with God, access into grace, and reconciliation. He died for the ungodly while they were sinners and enemies, and believers will be saved by his life. As the one man whose obedience and act of righteousness bring abundant grace, justification to life, and many made righteous, he is set against Adam, who foreshadows him.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: God commends his love toward us in that Christ died for us while we were yet sinners, and that love has been poured into believers' hearts through the Holy Spirit. He reconciled his enemies to himself through the death of his Son and will save believers from his wrath. His grace and gift abound to the many through Jesus Christ.

l: Adam, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Adam is the one man through whom sin entered the world, followed by death through sin. Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those whose sins were not like his disobedience. He is described as a foreshadowing of him who was to come, and his one trespass led to condemnation for all men and made many sinners.

l: believers (those in Christ Jesus), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Believers, justified by faith, have peace with God, access into grace, and rejoice in hope of God's glory and in their sufferings. They were weak, ungodly, sinners and enemies when Christ died for them, and they have now received reconciliation. They will be saved from wrath, and those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness will reign in life through Jesus Christ.

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Faith is the means by which believers are justified and through which they have access into the grace in which they stand. It leads to peace with God through Jesus Christ.

l: justification, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Believers are justified by faith and by Christ's blood, which brings peace with God and assurance of being saved from wrath. The free gift followed many trespasses to justification, and through one act of righteousness all men were justified to life.

l: grace, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Grace is the standing in which believers have access by faith, and it abounds to the many through the one man, Jesus Christ, much more than the trespass did. Where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly, so that grace might reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

l: sin, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Sin entered the world through one man, and all sinned, so death passed to all. Sin was in the world before the law but is not charged when there is no law, and the law came in so that the trespass might abound. Sin reigned in death, but grace abounded more where sin abounded.

l: death, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Death entered through sin and passed to all men because all sinned. It reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those whose sins weren't like Adam's disobedience, and reigned through the one trespass. Those who receive the abundance of grace will reign in life through Jesus Christ.

l: reconciliation, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Believers were reconciled to God while enemies, through the death of his Son. Being reconciled, they will be saved by his life, and they have now received the reconciliation through Jesus Christ, in whom they rejoice in God.

l: humanity (all men), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 5
s: Death passed to all men because all sinned, and through one trespass all men were condemned. Likewise, through one act of righteousness all men were justified to life. Through one man's disobedience many were made sinners, and through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: The chapter answers the question of whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may increase, and it answers with a firm no. It teaches that those baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death, buried with him, and will share his resurrection, so they should walk in newness of life. Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more, and believers are told to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God. The writer urges them not to let sin reign or to present their members to sin, but to present them to God as instruments of righteousness. He contrasts being servants of sin, which ends in death, with being servants of righteousness and of God, which brings sanctification and eternal life, and he closes by saying that the wages of sin is death while God's free gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: Christ Jesus is the one into whom believers were baptized, and they were baptized into his death. He was raised from the dead through the Father's glory, dies no more, and death no longer has dominion over him. He lives to God, and eternal life is given in him.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: God is the one to whom believers are to present themselves as alive from the dead, and to whom Christ lives. The Father's glory raised Christ from the dead. God is thanked for the readers' obedience, and he gives the free gift of eternal life in Christ Jesus.

l: sin, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: Sin is something believers died to and must not let reign in their mortal body or have their members as instruments of unrighteousness. It holds people in bondage as a master, and serving it leads to death. Its wages are death, and it will not have dominion over believers because they are under grace.

l: grace, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: Grace is the realm under which believers live rather than under law. The text rejects the idea of continuing in sin so that grace may abound, and it rejects sinning because of being under grace. Because of grace, sin will not have dominion over them.

l: believers (the readers addressed), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: The readers died to sin, were baptized into Christ's death, and were freed from bondage to sin, having become obedient from the heart to the form of teaching delivered to them. They are told to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and to present their members as servants of righteousness. Once ashamed of their former fruit, they now have the fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life.

l: baptism, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: Baptism is the means by which believers were baptized into Christ Jesus and into his death. Through it they were buried with him, so that they might walk in newness of life just as Christ was raised.

l: death, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: Death is the end of the things believers are now ashamed of and the result of serving sin. Christ died once to sin, and death no longer has dominion over him. Believers died with him and are thereby freed from sin, while the wages of sin is death.

l: Jesus's resurrection and death, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father. Believers united with him in the likeness of his death will also be part of his resurrection, and they believe they will live with him.

l: justification, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: Righteousness is what believers, freed from sin, became bondservants of, and it is the goal of obedience. They are told to present their members as instruments and servants of righteousness to God for sanctification. When they were servants of sin, they were free from righteousness.

l: eternal life, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 6
s: Eternal life is the result of being freed from sin and becoming servants of God. It is described as the free gift of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, in contrast to the death that is the wages of sin.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 7
s: The speaker addresses brothers who know the law, using the marriage analogy of a woman bound to her husband only while he lives to show that believers have died to the law through the body of Christ and are joined to him who was raised from the dead. He then asks whether the law is sin, answering that it is not, since the law revealed sin and coveting, while sin used the commandment to produce coveting, deceive, and kill him. The law is declared holy, righteous, and good, and sin is shown to be exceedingly sinful through it. The narrator describes an inner struggle in which he does what he hates and fails to do what he desires, attributing this to sin dwelling in his flesh and a law in his members warring against the law of his mind. He cries out for deliverance from the body of death, thanks God through Jesus Christ, and concludes that with his mind he serves God's law but with his flesh sin's law.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 7
s: The law has dominion over a person only as long as he lives, and believers have been discharged from it by dying to it. It is not sin but is holy, righteous, good, and spiritual; it made sin known, including coveting, though sin used its commandment to produce death. The narrator delights in it according to the inward person and serves it with his mind.

l: sin, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 7
s: Sin, finding occasion through the commandment, produced all kinds of coveting in the narrator, deceived him, and killed him. It is shown to be exceedingly sinful through the good commandment. It dwells in the narrator's flesh and works through a law in his members that wars against his mind and holds him captive.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 7
s: Through the body of Christ, believers were made dead to the law so they could be joined to him who was raised from the dead and bear fruit to God. He is also named as the one through whom the narrator thanks God, being called Jesus Christ, our Lord.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 7
s: God is the one to whom believers are to produce fruit, and whose law the narrator delights in and serves with his mind. The narrator thanks God through Jesus Christ for deliverance from the body of death.

l: narrator (the speaker, "I"), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 7
s: The narrator addresses the brothers, explains that he would not have known sin or coveting except through the law, and says he was once alive apart from the law but died when the commandment came. He describes doing what he hates and not doing what he desires, concluding that sin dwelling in his flesh is responsible. He cries out as a wretched man seeking deliverance, thanks God through Jesus Christ, and states that he serves God's law with his mind but sin's law with his flesh.

l: brothers (addressees), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 7
s: The brothers are addressed as men who know the law. They are told that they were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, joined to him who was raised from the dead, and discharged from the law so that they serve in newness of the spirit rather than oldness of the letter.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: This chapter declares that those in Christ Jesus face no condemnation, because the law of the Spirit of life has freed them from the law of sin and death, which God accomplished by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. It contrasts living according to the flesh, which brings death and hostility toward God, with living according to the Spirit, which brings life and peace. Those led by the Spirit are children of God and heirs with Christ, though they suffer now and wait with hope for adoption and the redemption of their bodies. The creation, subjected to vanity in hope, groans together with believers and awaits deliverance into the liberty of the glory of the children of God, while the Spirit helps believers' weakness by interceding for them. The chapter closes by affirming that God works all things for good for those who love him, that he foreknew, predestined, called, justified and glorified them, and that nothing can separate them from God's love in Christ Jesus.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: God did what the law could not do by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and condemning sin in the flesh. He raised Jesus from the dead, will give life to believers' mortal bodies, works all things together for good for those who love him, foreknew, predestined, called, justified and glorified those he chose, did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for all, and is the one who justifies.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: Jesus Christ is the one in whom there is no condemnation for believers, and God sent him as his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. He was raised from the dead by God, is at the right hand of God, and makes intercession for believers. He is the firstborn among many brothers, and believers are joint heirs with him.

l: Holy Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: The Spirit of God gives the law of life that frees from the law of sin and death, dwells in believers, and will give life to their mortal bodies. He leads God's children, gives the Spirit of adoption, testifies with believers' spirits that they are children of God, and helps their weakness by interceding for them with unutterable groanings according to God's will. Believers have the Spirit as first fruits.

l: flesh, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: The flesh is presented as the realm whose mind is death and is hostile toward God, not subject to God's law and unable to be. Those in the flesh cannot please God, and living after the flesh leads to death. The law was weak through the flesh, and God condemned sin in the flesh.

l: law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: The law could not accomplish what God did through his Son, because it was weak through the flesh. Its ordinance is fulfilled in those who walk according to the Spirit, and the mind of the flesh is not subject to it. The law of the Spirit of life is contrasted with the law of sin and of death.

l: believers (those in Christ Jesus), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: Believers face no condemnation, are freed from the law of sin and death, and are children of God, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ if they suffer with him. They groan and wait in hope for adoption and the redemption of their bodies, are helped by the Spirit, are called and justified, and are more than conquerors through Christ. Nothing can separate them from God's love in Christ Jesus.

l: creation, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: The creation waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed. It was subjected to vanity not by its own will but by him who subjected it, in hope of being delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. The whole creation groans and travails in pain until now.

l: love of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 8
s: The love of Christ is the thing from which the chapter asks who could separate believers, naming oppression, anguish, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril and sword. The text answers that believers are more than conquerors through him who loved them. Nothing, including death, life, angels, powers, height, depth or any created thing, can separate them from God's love in Christ Jesus.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: The speaker, Paul, declares in Christ that he feels great sorrow for his kinsmen the Israelites, even wishing himself accursed for their sake, and lists their privileges, including Christ coming from them according to the flesh. He argues that God's word has not failed, because not all who descend from Israel or Abraham are true children; the line runs through Isaac and Jacob by promise and election, not works. He answers the charge of unrighteousness by pointing to God's mercy toward Moses, the hardening of Pharaoh, and the potter's right over the clay, and says God endured vessels of wrath while making known the riches of his glory on vessels of mercy called from Jews and Gentiles. Citing Hosea and Isaiah, he shows that a remnant of Israel will be saved, and he concludes that Gentiles attained righteousness by faith while Israel, pursuing the law by works, stumbled over the stumbling stone laid in Zion.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: God is said to keep his word through promise and election: he chose Isaac and Jacob before birth, has mercy on whom he wills, hardens whom he wills, and holds a potter's right over the clay. He endured vessels of wrath with patience, prepared vessels of mercy for glory, called people from both Jews and Gentiles, and laid a stumbling stone in Zion.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: Christ is named as the one for whose sake Paul would wish himself accursed, and Paul speaks the truth in Christ. He came from the Israelites according to the flesh and is described as over all, God, blessed forever. The stumbling stone and rock of offense laid in Zion is tied to belief in him, and those who believe in him will not be disappointed.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: Paul affirms with his conscience in the Holy Spirit that he has great sorrow and unceasing pain for his brothers, and would wish himself accursed from Christ for their sake. He argues that God's word has not failed, answers the objections that God is unrighteous and finds fault, and explains why Israel stumbled while Gentiles attained righteousness.

l: Israel, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: The Israelites are described as possessing the adoption, glory, covenants, giving of the law, service, promises and the fathers, and as the people from whom Christ came according to the flesh. Not all who are of Israel are Israel; only a remnant will be saved, and Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not reach it because it sought it by works and stumbled over the stumbling stone.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: The Gentiles, who did not follow after righteousness, attained righteousness, namely the righteousness that is of faith. God also called some of his people from among them, in line with Hosea's words that those who were not his people would be called his people and children of the living God.

l: children of the promise, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: The children of the promise, not the children of the flesh, are counted as heirs and as children of God. This is shown by Isaac, born by a word of promise to Sarah, and by Rebekah's son Jacob, since Abraham's offspring are not all children and the offspring is accounted through Isaac.

l: divine election, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: God's purpose according to election stands not by works but by him who calls, as shown when Rebekah was told before her sons were born or had done good or bad that the elder would serve the younger. Paul cites 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' and says vessels of mercy were prepared beforehand for glory and called from Jews and Gentiles.

l: God's mercy and hardening, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: God declares to Moses that he will have mercy on whom he has mercy, so the outcome depends not on human will or running but on God. Pharaoh was raised up to display God's power and proclaim his name, and Paul concludes that God has mercy on whom he desires and hardens whom he desires, rejecting the objection that this makes God unrighteous.

l: justification, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 9
s: Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness attained the righteousness of faith, while Israel, following a law of righteousness, did not arrive at it. The reason given is that Israel did not seek it by faith but as if by works, and so stumbled over the stumbling stone, while those who believe in him will not be disappointed.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 10
s: The speaker, addressing his brothers, expresses his heart's desire and prayer that Israel be saved, testifying that they have zeal for God but without knowledge. He says they sought to establish their own righteousness and did not submit to God's righteousness, while Christ is the fulfillment of the law for everyone who believes. Contrasting Moses' righteousness of the law with the righteousness of faith, he says the word is near, in the mouth and heart, and that confessing Jesus as Lord and believing God raised him from the dead brings salvation. He states there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, since the same Lord is rich to all who call on him, and then traces the sequence of calling, believing, hearing, preaching, and being sent. He concludes that although the message went out to all the earth, Israel did not all listen and remained a disobedient and contrary people, while those who did not seek God found him.

l: Israel, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 10
s: Israel is the object of the speaker's heart's desire and prayer for salvation. They have zeal for God but not according to knowledge, were ignorant of God's righteousness, sought to establish their own, and did not subject themselves to God's righteousness. Though they heard and were warned of provocation by a non-nation, God says he stretched out his hands all day to them as a disobedient and contrary people.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 10
s: God is the one to whom the speaker prays for Israel's salvation and whose righteousness Israel failed to submit to. He raised Christ from the dead, and in Isaiah's words he was found by those who didn't seek him and stretched out his hands all day to a disobedient and contrary people.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 10
s: Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. No one needs to ascend to heaven to bring him down or descend into the abyss to bring him up from the dead, and God raised him from the dead. Confessing Jesus as Lord is part of being saved.

l: righteousness of God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 10
s: Two kinds are contrasted: Israel's own righteousness, which they sought to establish, and God's righteousness, to which they did not submit. Moses writes of the righteousness of the law, where the one who does the commands lives by them, while the righteousness of faith speaks of the near word. With the heart one believes resulting in righteousness.

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 10
s: The righteousness of faith says the word is near, in the mouth and heart, which is the word of faith that is preached. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. Not all listened, as Isaiah asks who has believed the report.

l: salvation, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 10
s: Salvation is the speaker's prayer for Israel. It comes to those who confess with the mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in the heart that God raised him from the dead, and to whoever calls on the name of the Lord. Confession is made resulting in salvation.

l: believers (everyone who believes), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 10
s: Everyone who believes receives righteousness through Christ, the fulfillment of the law, and will not be disappointed. There is no distinction between Jew and Greek, since the same Lord is rich to all who call on him. They come to believe by hearing the preached word from those who are sent.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: The writer, who identifies himself as an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin and an apostle to the Gentiles, argues that God has not rejected his people Israel. He points to a remnant chosen by grace, as in the days of Elijah, while the rest were hardened. Israel's fall has brought salvation to the Gentiles, and this is meant to provoke Israel to jealousy. Using the image of an olive tree, he warns Gentile believers, grafted in as a wild olive, not to boast over the broken-off natural branches, since God can graft them in again. He declares that a partial hardening has come on Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, that all Israel will be saved, and that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable, ending with praise of God's wisdom.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: God did not reject his people whom he foreknew, and he reserved seven thousand men who had not bowed to Baal. He gave the hardened a spirit of stupor, shows both goodness and severity, is able to graft broken branches in again, and has bound all to disobedience so that he might have mercy on all. His gifts and calling are irrevocable, and all things are of him, through him, and to him.

l: Israel, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: Israel did not obtain what it sought, while the chosen obtained it and the rest were hardened. Its fall brought salvation to the Gentiles and riches to the world, and a partial hardening has come on it until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in. The text says all Israel will be saved, and that they are enemies for the Gentiles' sake regarding the Good News but beloved for the fathers' sake regarding election.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: The writer says he is an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham of the tribe of Benjamin, and an apostle to the Gentiles whose ministry he glorifies. He hopes to provoke his own flesh to jealousy and save some of them. He tells the Gentile readers of the mystery of Israel's partial hardening so they will not be wise in their own conceits.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: The Gentiles received salvation through Israel's fall, and are pictured as a wild olive grafted in among the branches, sharing the root and richness of the olive tree. They are warned not to boast or be conceited, because they stand by faith and will be cut off if they do not continue in God's goodness. Their fullness must come in before Israel's hardening ends, and they obtained mercy through Israel's disobedience.

l: remnant, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: A remnant exists at the present time according to the election of grace, paralleling the seven thousand men God reserved in Elijah's day who had not bowed to Baal. The chosen ones within Israel obtained what Israel sought, while the rest were hardened.

l: olive tree, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: The olive tree is the image in which the root is holy and the branches are holy. Some natural branches were broken off by unbelief, and Gentiles, a wild olive, were grafted in to share the root and richness. The natural branches can be grafted back into their own tree if they do not continue in unbelief.

l: grace, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: The remnant exists according to the election of grace. The text states that if election is by grace it is no longer of works, otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

l: hardening of Israel, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: Those of Israel other than the chosen were hardened, in accord with Scripture that God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear. It is described as partial and lasting until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, after which all Israel will be saved.

l: salvation, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 11
s: Salvation has come to the Gentiles by Israel's fall, intended to provoke Israel to jealousy. The writer hopes to save some of his own people, and says all Israel will be saved when the Deliverer comes out of Zion and takes away their sins.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: The writer urges the brothers, by the mercies of God, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice and to be transformed rather than conformed to this world, so they may prove God's will. He tells everyone not to think too highly of themselves, since God has apportioned each a measure of faith. Believers are described as many members forming one body in Christ, each with differing gifts such as prophecy, service, teaching, exhorting, giving, ruling, and showing mercy, to be exercised faithfully. The chapter then lists practical commands: love without hypocrisy, hating evil and clinging to good, honoring one another, enduring troubles, showing hospitality, blessing persecutors, and rejoicing and weeping with others. It closes by forbidding revenge, leaving vengeance to God, calling for feeding one's enemy, and urging believers to overcome evil with good.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: God is the one by whose mercies the brothers are urged to present themselves, and whose good, well-pleasing, and perfect will they are to prove. He has apportioned a measure of faith to each person. He claims vengeance for himself, saying he will repay, so believers should give place to his wrath.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: Christ is the one in whom the many believers are one body. Individually they are members of one another in him.

l: brothers (the addressees), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: The brothers are urged to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, to be transformed by renewing their minds, and to think of themselves reasonably. They receive a series of commands on love, humility, hospitality, peace, blessing persecutors, and refusing revenge, ending with the charge to overcome evil with good.

l: this world, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: This world is the pattern believers are told not to be conformed to. Transformation by the renewing of the mind is set against it.

l: body of Christ (the church as one body), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: The many believers are compared to one body with many members that do not all have the same function. They are one body in Christ and members of one another.

l: spiritual gifts, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: Gifts differ according to the grace given to believers. The text names prophecy, service, teaching, exhorting, giving, ruling, and showing mercy. Each is to be used faithfully: prophecy in proportion to faith, giving with generosity, ruling with diligence, and mercy with cheerfulness.

l: living sacrifice (the believers' bodies), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: Believers are urged to present their bodies as a living sacrifice that is holy and acceptable to God. The text calls this their spiritual service.

l: love, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: Love is to be without hypocrisy. It shows in tender affection among the brothers, preferring one another in honor, and blessing rather than cursing persecutors.

l: evil, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: Evil is something believers are told to abhor and never to repay with evil. They are not to be overcome by it but to overcome it with good.

l: the good (those who do good), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 12
s: Good is what believers are told to cling to. It is the means by which evil is to be overcome, including feeding a hungry enemy and giving him a drink.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 13
s: Chapter 13 instructs the readers to be in subjection to the higher authorities, since all authority is from God and resisting it means withstanding God's ordinance and receiving judgment. Rulers are described as God's servants who are a terror to evil but bring praise for good, bearing the sword against wrongdoers, so the readers are to submit for conscience' sake as well as because of wrath. The readers are told to pay taxes, customs, respect, and honor to whom they are owed. They are to owe no one anything except love, which fulfills the law because it sums up the commandments against adultery, murder, stealing, and coveting and does no harm to a neighbor. The chapter closes with a call to awaken because salvation is nearer, to throw off deeds of darkness, walk properly as in the day, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ without making provision for the flesh.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 13
s: God is named as the source of all authority, and the existing authorities are ordained by him. Rulers are called his servants, who bring good to the obedient and act as avengers of wrath against those who do evil.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 13
s: In the final verse, the readers are exhorted to put on the Lord Jesus Christ as the alternative to making provision for the flesh and its lusts.

l: higher authorities, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 13
s: The higher authorities are said to exist only from God and to be ordained by him. They are described as servants of God who are not a terror to good work but to evil, who bear the sword not in vain, and who receive taxes as God's service.

l: Roman believers (the letter's recipients), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 13
s: The readers are told to be in subjection to the authorities, to pay taxes, customs, respect, and honor as owed, and to owe nothing except love. They are urged to awaken from sleep, throw off the deeds of darkness, put on the armor of light, walk properly as in the day, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

l: love, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 13
s: Love is the one debt the readers are to owe each other, and it does no harm to a neighbor. It sums up the commandments in the saying to love your neighbor as yourself, and is therefore the fulfillment of the law.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 13
s: The commandments against adultery, murder, stealing, and coveting, along with any others, are all summed up in the saying to love your neighbor as yourself. The one who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law, and love is its fulfillment.

l: subjection to authority, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 13
s: Subjection is commanded of every soul, because resisting authority means withstanding God's ordinance and brings judgment. The readers are to submit not only because of wrath but also for conscience' sake, which includes paying taxes and giving respect and honor as owed.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 14
s: Chapter 14 instructs believers to accept the one who is weak in faith without quarreling over opinions, specifically about eating only vegetables and observing certain days. Those who eat and those who abstain are told not to despise or judge each other, since each answers to the Lord, and all will stand before Christ's judgment seat and give account to God. The text states that nothing is unclean of itself, yet believers must not grieve or cause a brother to stumble by their food, and should pursue peace and mutual building up because God's Kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Whoever eats with doubt is condemned because it is not of faith. The chapter closes with a doxology to the only wise God through Jesus Christ, who establishes believers according to the Good News and the revealed mystery.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 14
s: God has accepted both the one who eats and the one who doesn't, and has power to make his servant stand. Every knee will bow to him and every tongue confess to him, and each person will give account of himself to God. The chapter ends by calling him the only wise God, the eternal God whose commandment makes the mystery known to all nations.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 14
s: Christ died, rose, and lived again so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. All will stand before his judgment seat, and he is the one for whom a brother is said to have died. Paul is persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean of itself, and glory is ascribed to God through Jesus Christ.

l: one who is weak in faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 14
s: He is to be accepted, though not for disputes over opinions, and he eats only vegetables. He is told not to judge the one who eats, for God has accepted that person, and he is warned that if he eats while doubting, he is condemned because it is not of faith.

l: one who has faith to eat all things, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 14
s: He has faith to eat all things and is told not to despise the one who abstains. He is urged not to destroy a brother with his food or cause a stumbling block, and to keep his own faith between himself and God. Though all things are clean, it is evil for him to cause stumbling by eating.

l: brother (the fellow believer), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 14
s: The brother is someone for whom Christ died, and no one should judge or despise him. He must not be grieved, made to stumble, offended, or weakened by another's food, and believers are to build one another up toward peace.

l: judging and despising others, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 14
s: Judging and despising are forbidden: the one who eats must not despise the one who doesn't, and the one who doesn't must not judge the one who eats. The text asks why one would judge or despise a brother, since all will stand before Christ's judgment seat and each will give account to God. Believers are told instead to judge only that no one puts a stumbling block in a brother's way.

l: dietary practices (eating food, meat, wine), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 14
s: Some eat all things while others eat only vegetables, and each does so to the Lord, giving God thanks. Nothing is unclean of itself, but it is unclean to one who considers it so, and God's Kingdom is not eating and drinking but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine if it makes a brother stumble, and eating with doubt is sin because it is not of faith.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: In Romans 15, Paul urges the strong among the Roman believers to bear with the weak, please their neighbors, and accept one another as Christ accepted them, citing Christ's example and the Scriptures. He explains that Christ became a servant of the circumcision to confirm the promises to the fathers so that the Gentiles might glorify God, supporting this with quotations from Scripture. Paul describes his own ministry as a priestly servant of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, having fully preached the Good News from Jerusalem around to Illyricum and aiming to preach where Christ was not yet named. He announces that he is going to Jerusalem with a contribution from Macedonia and Achaia for the poor saints, and afterward plans to travel by way of the Romans to Spain. He asks the Romans to strive with him in prayer for deliverance from the disobedient in Judea and for his service to be acceptable, and closes with a blessing of peace.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: Christ did not please himself, and he accepted the believers to the glory of God. He was made a servant of the circumcision to confirm the promises to the fathers and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. Paul boasts in him and says Christ worked through Paul by word and deed for the obedience of the Gentiles.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: God is called the God of perseverance and encouragement, of hope, and of peace, and is asked to grant the believers like-mindedness and to fill them with joy and peace. He gave grace to Paul to serve among the Gentiles, and the Gentiles are to glorify him for his mercy. His will is the means by which Paul hopes to come to Rome in joy.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: Paul says he writes boldly as a reminder, as a servant of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles and a priest of the Good News, having preached fully from Jerusalem around to Illyricum without building on another's foundation. He explains he was often hindered from visiting Rome, plans to go to Spain by way of Rome after delivering the contribution to Jerusalem, and begs the believers to pray for his deliverance from the disobedient in Judea.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: Scripture quotations say the Gentiles will praise God, rejoice with his people, and hope in the root of Jesse who arises to rule over them. Paul says their offering is made acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Having shared in the spiritual things of the Jerusalem saints, they owe them service in material things, which Macedonia and Achaia have done.

l: Roman believers (the letter's recipients), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: The Roman believers are urged to bear with the weak, please their neighbors for good, be of the same mind, and accept one another as Christ accepted them. Paul is persuaded they are full of goodness and knowledge and able to admonish others. He hopes to visit them on his way to Spain, to be helped on his way by them, and asks them to strive with him in prayer.

l: saints at Jerusalem, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: The saints at Jerusalem include the poor among them, for whom Macedonia and Achaia gladly made a contribution. The Gentiles are described as their debtors because they have shared in their spiritual things. Paul hopes his service will be acceptable to them.

l: Jerusalem, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: Paul says he is going to Jerusalem to serve the saints, and it is the starting point of the region in which he has fully preached the Good News as far as Illyricum. He asks for prayer that his service for Jerusalem be acceptable.

l: Spain, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: Spain is named as Paul's next destination, since he has no more place in the regions where he has worked. He hopes to see the Roman believers on his way there and be helped onward by them.

l: the Good News, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: The Good News of God and of Christ is what Paul serves as a priest, and he has fully preached it from Jerusalem around to Illyricum. He aims to preach it where Christ was not already named. He expects to come to Rome in the fullness of its blessing.

l: contribution for the poor saints, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: Macedonia and Achaia gladly made a certain contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem. Paul presents it as a debt the Gentiles owe for sharing in spiritual things, and he intends to deliver it and seal this fruit to them before going on to Spain.

l: Paul's planned journey to Rome and Spain, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 15
s: Paul plans to go to Spain and visit the Roman believers on the way, hoping to be helped onward by them after enjoying their company. This follows first going to Jerusalem to deliver the contribution. He asks for prayer that he may come in joy through God's will and find rest with them.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: The chapter opens with Paul commending Phoebe, a servant of the assembly at Cenchreae, and asking the recipients to receive and assist her. He then sends a long series of greetings to named individuals and households, including Prisca and Aquila, who risked their necks for his life, and Andronicus and Junia, who are notable among the apostles. Paul urges the brothers to watch out for and turn away from those who cause divisions and stumbling, saying they serve their own belly and deceive the innocent. He promises that the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under their feet. The chapter closes with greetings from Timothy, Lucius, Jason, Sosipater, Tertius (who wrote the letter), Gaius, Erastus and Quartus, and a final blessing of grace.

l: Phoebe, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: Phoebe is commended by Paul as our sister and a servant of the assembly at Cenchreae. The recipients are asked to receive her in the Lord worthily and assist her in whatever she needs, since she has been a helper of many, including Paul himself.

l: Prisca, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: Prisca is greeted by Paul along with Aquila as his fellow worker in Christ Jesus. Together they risked their own necks for his life, and all the assemblies of the Gentiles give thanks to them. The assembly in their house is also greeted.

l: Aquila, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: Aquila is greeted by Paul together with Prisca as his fellow worker in Christ Jesus. They risked their own necks for Paul's life and receive thanks from Paul and from all the Gentile assemblies. An assembly meets in their house.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: Paul commends Phoebe, greets many named people with personal descriptions, and urges the brothers to turn away from those causing divisions. He rejoices over the recipients' known obedience and wants them wise in good and innocent in evil. He also relays greetings from his companions and closes with a blessing of grace.

l: Roman believers (the letter's recipients), Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: The recipients are asked to receive and assist Phoebe, to greet one another with a holy kiss, and to look out for and turn away from those causing divisions. Their obedience is said to have become known to all, and Paul rejoices over them and desires that they be wise in good and innocent in evil. They are promised that the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under their feet.

l: divisive people, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: Those who cause divisions and occasions of stumbling contrary to the doctrine the recipients learned are to be watched and turned away from. Paul says they do not serve Christ but their own belly, and deceive the hearts of the innocent with smooth and flattering speech.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: Jesus Christ is named as the one in whom Paul's fellow workers labor, and the one whom the divisive people fail to serve. The assemblies of Christ send greetings. His grace is invoked on the recipients at the close of the chapter.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: God is called the God of peace, who will quickly crush Satan under the feet of the recipients.

l: Tertius, Paul’s Letter to the Romans, Chapter 16
s: Tertius identifies himself as the one who writes the letter and sends his own greeting in the Lord.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, together with Sosthenes, greets the assembly of God at Corinth and gives thanks for the grace and gifts given them in Christ Jesus, affirming that God is faithful and will confirm them blameless until the day of the Lord. Paul then begs them to be united, because people from Chloe's household reported contentions in which members claimed to follow Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. He recalls that he baptized only Crispus, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas, and says Christ sent him to preach the Good News rather than to baptize. He argues that the word of the cross seems foolishness to those who are dying but is the power of God to those being saved, and that God has made the wisdom of the world foolish. God chose the foolish, weak, and lowly so that no flesh would boast before him, and anyone who boasts should boast in the Lord.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, called to be an apostle through the will of God, writes with Sosthenes to the Corinthians, thanks God for them, and begs them to end their divisions. He says he baptized only Crispus, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas, because Christ sent him to preach the Good News not in wisdom of words, and he preaches Christ crucified.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: The assembly is addressed as those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called saints, enriched in all speech and knowledge and lacking in no gift. It is reported to have contentions, with members saying they follow Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ, and it is reminded that not many of its members were wise, mighty, or noble according to the flesh.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is called Lord and Son of God, and the Corinthians were called into fellowship with him and will be confirmed blameless in his day. Paul asks whether Christ is divided, preaches him as crucified, and describes him as the power and wisdom of God, made to believers wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: God is described as faithful, having called the Corinthians into fellowship with his Son and given them grace. He chose the foolish, weak, lowly, and despised things of the world to shame the wise and strong, so that no flesh would boast before him, and he was pleased to save believers through the foolishness of the preaching.

l: divisions and contentions in Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Paul learned from those of Chloe's household that contentions existed among the Corinthians, with groups saying they follow Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. Paul begs them to speak the same thing and be perfected in the same mind and judgment, and rebukes the divisions with questions about whether Christ is divided and whether Paul was crucified for them.

l: cross of Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying but the power of God to those being saved. Paul preaches Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks, and says he preaches not in wisdom of words so that the cross wouldn't be made void.

l: wisdom of the world, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: The text says God will destroy the wisdom of the wise and has made the wisdom of this world foolish, since the world through its wisdom didn't know God. Greeks seek after wisdom, but the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and God chose the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: In this chapter the speaker, addressing the brothers, says he came to them without eloquence or human wisdom, determined to know only Jesus Christ and him crucified, and he came in weakness, fear, and trembling. His preaching demonstrated the Spirit and power so that their faith would rest on God's power rather than men's wisdom. He says he speaks God's hidden, foreordained wisdom among the full grown, which the rulers of this world did not know, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. God reveals these things through the Spirit, who searches the deep things of God and teaches the words spoken. The natural man cannot receive or discern them, while the spiritual person discerns all things, and believers have Christ's mind.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: Jesus Christ, crucified, is the one thing the speaker determined to know among the brothers. He is called the Lord of glory, whom the rulers of this world crucified because they did not know God's wisdom. Believers are said to have his mind.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: God foreordained his wisdom before the worlds for the glory of believers and has prepared things beyond what eye, ear, or heart has perceived for those who love him. He revealed these things to the speaker and others through the Spirit. No one knows the things of God except God's Spirit, and the faith of the brothers is meant to stand in his power.

l: Holy Spirit, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: The Spirit searches all things, including the deep things of God, and is the one who knows God's things. God revealed his hidden wisdom through the Spirit, and the Spirit teaches the words the speaker uses. The Spirit is from God and was received by believers so they might know what God freely gave them; his things are spiritually discerned.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: The speaker recounts coming to the brothers without excellence of speech or wisdom, in weakness, fear, and much trembling, proclaiming God's testimony. His preaching was a demonstration of the Spirit and power, not persuasive words of human wisdom. He speaks God's wisdom among the full grown, in words taught by the Holy Spirit.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: The brothers are those to whom the speaker came, determined to know only Jesus Christ crucified. The speaker wanted their faith to rest on the power of God rather than the wisdom of men. They are included among those who received the Spirit from God and can know what God has freely given.

l: God's wisdom, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: God's wisdom is spoken in a mystery among the full grown. It was hidden and foreordained before the worlds for believers' glory, and the rulers of this world did not know it. It is revealed through the Spirit and is spiritually discerned, appearing as foolishness to the natural man.

l: human wisdom, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: Human wisdom is contrasted with God's wisdom: the speaker did not use persuasive words of it, so that faith would not rest on the wisdom of men. It is described as the wisdom of this world and its rulers, who are coming to nothing. The words the speaker uses are not taught by it but by the Holy Spirit.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The writer, Paul, tells the Corinthian believers that he could not address them as spiritual but only as fleshly babies in Christ, fed with milk rather than solid food. Their jealousy, strife, and factions, in which some say they follow Paul and others Apollos, show they are still fleshly. Paul and Apollos are only servants, one planting and one watering, while God gives the increase. The believers are God's farming, building, and temple, and Paul laid the foundation, Jesus Christ, on which others build work that fire on the Day will test. The chapter closes by warning against worldly wisdom and boasting in men, since all things belong to the believers, who are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Paul says he could not speak to the Corinthians as spiritual people and fed them milk instead of solid food. He describes himself as a servant who planted, and as a wise master builder who laid a foundation by the grace of God given to him. He is one of the men the Corinthians wrongly boast in, though all things, including Paul, are theirs.

l: Apollos, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Apollos is named as a figure some Corinthians claim to follow, and Paul calls him a servant through whom they believed. He watered what Paul planted, and he and Paul are the same, each receiving his own reward according to his own labor. He is listed among the things that belong to the believers.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: God gave the increase to what Paul planted and Apollos watered, so only God who gives the increase is anything. The believers are his fellow workers, his farming, building, and temple, and he will destroy anyone who destroys his temple. He regards the wisdom of this world as foolishness and knows the reasoning of the wise to be worthless. Christ is God's.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ is identified as the one foundation that has been laid, and no one can lay any other. The believers are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The Corinthians are rebuked as fleshly babies in Christ, not yet ready for solid food, because of their jealousy, strife, and factions. They are told they are God's fellow workers, farming, building, and temple, in whom God's Spirit lives. They are urged not to boast in men, since all things are theirs, and they are Christ's.

l: foundation (laid by Paul, Jesus Christ), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Paul, as a wise master builder, laid the foundation by the grace of God, and it is Jesus Christ. No one can lay any other foundation, though others build on it and must be careful how they do so.

l: divisions and contentions in Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Factions appear among the Corinthians as some say they follow Paul and others Apollos. Paul cites these, along with jealousy and strife, as evidence that the believers are fleshly and walk in the ways of men.

l: each man's work (building on the foundation), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Each man's work, built on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or straw, will be revealed by the Day and tested by fire. If it remains, the builder receives a reward. If it is burned, he suffers loss but is himself saved, as through fire.

l: worldly wisdom, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The wisdom of this world is declared foolishness with God, and anyone who thinks himself wise in it must become a fool in order to become wise. Scripture is cited that God takes the wise in their craftiness and knows their reasoning is worthless.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: In Chapter 4, the writer, speaking for himself and Apollos, asks that he and his fellow workers be regarded as Christ's servants and stewards of God's mysteries, who must be found faithful. He says he does not care about being judged by the Corinthians or any human court, and that he does not even judge himself, because the Lord is his judge and will reveal hidden things and the counsels of hearts. He rebukes the Corinthians for being puffed up and boasting of what they received, contrasting their self-satisfied reigning with the apostles' hunger, dishonor, and suffering as a spectacle to the world. He calls them his beloved children, says he became their father in Christ Jesus through the Good News, urges them to imitate him, and announces that he is sending Timothy to remind them of his ways. He warns that he will come shortly, if the Lord is willing, to test the power of the puffed-up, and asks whether they want him to come with a rod or in love and gentleness.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: Paul asks to be regarded as a servant of Christ and steward of God's mysteries, and says he cares little about human judgment, not even judging himself, since the Lord is his judge. He describes the apostles' suffering, calls the Corinthians his beloved children whose father in Christ Jesus he became through the Good News, and urges them to imitate him. He sends Timothy ahead and says he will come shortly, if the Lord is willing, asking whether they want him to come with a rod or in love and gentleness.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: Christ is the one whose servants the apostles are, and for whose sake they are fools. Paul became the Corinthians' father in Christ Jesus through the Good News, and Timothy will remind them of Paul's ways which are in Christ.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: God is the one whose mysteries the apostles steward, and from whom each person will receive praise. He is said to have displayed the apostles last of all, like men sentenced to death, and his Kingdom is said to consist not in word but in power.

l: Lord, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: The Lord is named as the one who judges Paul and who will come to bring hidden things of darkness to light and reveal the counsels of hearts. Paul's coming to Corinth depends on the Lord's willingness.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: The Corinthian believers are told not to judge before the time and are rebuked for being puffed up, boasting of what they received, and acting as if already rich and reigning.
