They are contrasted with the suffering apostles, addressed as Paul's beloved children, urged to imitate him, and asked whether they want him to come with a rod or in gentleness.

l: the apostles, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: The apostles are presented as stewards who must be faithful, displayed last of all like men sentenced to death, and made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men. They are described as fools, weak, and dishonored, hungry, thirsty, naked, beaten, homeless, and toiling with their own hands, blessing those who curse them and enduring persecution.

l: judgment, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: Paul says human judgment of him is a very small thing and that he does not even judge himself, because the Lord is his judge. The Corinthians are told to judge nothing before the Lord comes, who will expose hidden things and the counsels of hearts, after which each will receive praise from God.

l: pride and boasting, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: Paul says the Corinthians are puffed up against one another and asks what they have that they did not receive, questioning why they boast. He says some are puffed up as though he would not come, and that he will test not their words but their power.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: In Chapter 5, the author addresses a report of sexual immorality among the Corinthian believers, in which a man has his father's wife, a sin not even named among the Gentiles. He rebukes the believers for being arrogant instead of mourning, and says that though absent in body he has already judged the man and directs them to deliver him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh so the spirit may be saved. He uses the image of yeast, which leavens the whole lump, to urge them to purge out the old yeast and keep the feast with sincerity and truth, since Christ, the Passover, has been sacrificed. He clarifies an earlier letter: they are not to avoid the sexual sinners of the world, but not to associate or even eat with a professing brother who is immoral, covetous, an idolater, a slanderer, a drunkard, or an extortionist. God judges those outside, while the believers are to judge those within and put away the wicked man.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Paul, absent in body but present in spirit, says he has already judged the man who has his father's wife. He rebukes the Corinthians for their arrogance and clarifies his earlier letter's instruction about associating with sexual sinners, saying he has no part in judging outsiders but expects the believers to judge those within.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: The Corinthian believers are rebuked for being arrogant and boasting rather than mourning over the sin among them. They are told to gather, deliver the man to Satan, purge the old yeast, keep the feast with sincerity and truth, not associate with immoral brothers, and put away the wicked man from among themselves.

l: man who has his father's wife, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: This man is reported to have his father's wife, and Paul has already judged him. The believers are instructed to deliver him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus, and to put him away from among them.

l: sexual immorality, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Sexual immorality is reported among the Corinthians, of a kind not even named among the Gentiles, namely a man having his father's wife. Paul says he previously wrote not to have company with sexual sinners, clarifying that this means professing brothers rather than the sexual sinners of the world.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Jesus Christ is named as the Lord in whose name and with whose power the believers are to gather and deliver the offender to Satan. He is called "our Passover," who has been sacrificed in our place, and the day of the Lord Jesus is when the man's spirit may be saved.

l: yeast, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Yeast serves as a metaphor: a little yeast leavens the whole lump, illustrating how one sinner's influence affects the community. Believers are told to purge out the old yeast and to keep the feast not with the yeast of malice and wickedness but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

l: erring brothers (immoral believers), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Anyone called a brother who is a sexual sinner, covetous, an idolater, a slanderer, a drunkard, or an extortionist is not to be associated with, and the believers are not even to eat with such a person. Unlike outsiders, whom God judges, these within the community are to be judged by the believers.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The writer rebukes the believers for taking lawsuits against one another before unbelievers instead of settling matters within the assembly, arguing that the saints will judge the world and angels and so should be able to decide small disputes. He says it is already a defect to have lawsuits and that they would do better to be wronged or defrauded, yet they themselves wrong and defraud their brothers. He warns that the unrighteous, including those listed in a catalogue of sins, will not inherit God's Kingdom, and reminds them that some of them were once such people but were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and the Spirit of God. He then addresses bodily conduct, insisting that the body is for the Lord and not for sexual immorality, that believers' bodies are members of Christ, and that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought with a price, so they must glorify God in it.

l: saints, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The saints are said to be the ones who will judge the world and even angels. On this basis the writer argues they should be fit to judge smaller matters of this life, rather than going before the unrighteous.

l: the unrighteous, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The unrighteous are those before whom believers wrongly take their lawsuits, and the writer describes them as of no account in the assembly. They will not inherit God's Kingdom, and a list of sins, including sexual immorality, idolatry, theft, drunkenness and extortion, characterizes them.

l: lawsuits among believers, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The writer condemns brother going to law with brother before unbelievers, shaming the readers for lacking someone wise enough to decide between brothers. He calls such lawsuits already a defect and says it would be better to be wronged or defrauded.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: Brothers are the fellow believers who are suing one another and, according to the writer, wronging and defrauding each other. The text suggests a wise man among them should be able to decide between them.

l: Corinthian believers (the readers), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The readers are rebuked and shamed for their lawsuits before unbelievers and for wronging and defrauding their brothers. They are warned not to be deceived about the unrighteous, reminded that some of them were once such people but were washed, sanctified and justified, and urged to flee sexual immorality and glorify God in their bodies.

l: God’s Kingdom, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: God's Kingdom is said not to be inherited by the unrighteous, a point stated twice and illustrated by a list including the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, drunkards, slanderers and extortionists.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: God will bring to nothing the belly and foods, raised up the Lord, and will raise believers up by his power. Believers' bodies and spirits are his, and they were bought with a price, so they are to glorify him.

l: Jesus, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: Jesus is called the Lord, in whose name the readers were justified. God raised him up, believers' bodies are members of Christ, and the one joined to the Lord is one spirit with him.

l: Holy Spirit, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The Holy Spirit is described as living in believers, whose body is his temple, and as given to them from God. Believers were also justified in the Spirit of God.

l: sexual immorality, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: Sexual immorality is listed among behaviors that exclude people from God's Kingdom, and the readers are told to flee it. The writer argues the body is not for it but for the Lord, and that joining with a prostitute makes members of Christ one body with her, so the person sins against his own body.

l: body, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The body is said to be for the Lord and not for sexual immorality, and God will raise it up. It is a member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit, and because believers were bought with a price they are to glorify God in it.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: In Chapter 7, Paul answers questions the Corinthians wrote to him about marriage and related matters. He says it is good not to touch a woman, yet urges each man and woman to have a spouse because of sexual immorality, and that husband and wife owe each other affection and authority over each other's bodies. He commands that married believers not separate, gives his own judgment about marriages with unbelievers, and allows separation if the unbeliever departs. He teaches that each person should remain in the calling in which he was called, whether circumcised, uncircumcised, bondservant or free. He advises the unmarried, virgins and widows to remain as they are because of the present distress and the shortness of time, while affirming that marrying is not sin, so that believers may attend to the Lord without distraction.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Paul answers the Corinthians' written questions, wishing all were as he is while acknowledging that each has his own gift from God. He distinguishes his own judgment and concession from the Lord's command, and closes by saying he thinks he also has God's Spirit.

l: Lord, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: The Lord is the source of the command that a wife not leave her husband and a husband not leave his wife, which Paul distinguishes from his own opinions. The unmarried are said to be concerned with pleasing the Lord, and a bondservant called in the Lord is the Lord's free man.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: God gives each person his own gift and calls each in a particular condition, and he has called believers in peace. Paul says that keeping God's commandments is what matters, and that believers should stay in their condition with God.

l: marriage, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Marriage is presented as a remedy for sexual immorality and lack of self-control, since it is better to marry than to burn with passion. Marrying is not sin, but Paul says it brings oppression in the flesh and divided concern, so he regards remaining unmarried as better. A wife is bound as long as her husband lives.

l: husbands, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Husbands are told to give their wives the affection owed them and are told they have no authority over their own bodies, but the wife does. They are commanded not to leave their wives, including unbelieving wives who are content to stay. A married man is concerned about how to please his wife.

l: wives, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Wives are told to give husbands the affection owed them and not to leave them, and the wife has no authority over her own body, but the husband does. If a wife departs, she must remain unmarried or be reconciled. A widow is free to marry whomever she desires, only in the Lord, though Paul thinks she is happier if she stays as she is.
